artists.biography:
The group was formed by guitarist, singer and chief songwriter Bill Fisher and keyboardist Michael Wetherburn over a mutual love of musical theatre and Queen. The group members had previously played in various bands in and around Nottingham, and a number of early songs by the group had been written years before while in other bands. Fisher was more interested in progressive pop rather than progressive rock, and wanted the band to be primarily about good songwriting over pointless technical ability. His influences include The Beatles, Kate Bush, David Bowie and Peter Gabriel, The instrumentation makes prominent use of the Hammond organ.

The band is signed to Bilocation Records. They have also covered Pink Floyd's "The Trial" on Magnetic Eye Records' tribute album The Wall Redux. Fisher has described the group as a "twofold entity: a new religious movement…and a 7-piece supergroup".

In 2017, the group released "Evil in your Eye" from their first album Is Satan Real? on 21 August to coincide with the solar eclipse on the same day.
Bill Fisher - guitar, vocals
Joanne Joyce - vocals
Caroline Cawley - vocals
Michael Wetherburn - keyboards, vocals
Amy Nicholson - cello, vocals
Sam Lloyd - bass
Loz Stone - drums

perplexity.description:
Everybody's Going To Die" is the third studio album by Church of the Cosmic Skull, released in 2019 on the band's own label, Septaphonic Records. Musically, the album blends elements of psychedelic rock, progressive rock, and theatrical pop, characterized by lush vocal harmonies, intricate arrangements, and a playful yet philosophical lyrical approach. The band's signature use of multiple vocalists and layered instrumentation creates a rich, dynamic sound that draws comparisons to acts like Queen and Queens of the Stone Age, while maintaining a distinct identity rooted in their conceptual and thematic explorations.

Within the band's discography, "Everybody's Going To Die" stands as a pivotal release, marking their transition to independent label ownership and further solidifying their reputation for ambitious, genre-blurring rock music. The album tackles themes such as mortality, the cult of personality, social media echo chambers, and the pursuit of fame, all delivered with a mix of wit and introspection. It received positive critical reception, with Mojo magazine noting its appeal to fans of classic and modern prog, and broadcaster Jonathan Ross praising the band's unique take on the genre. The album's success helped expand Church of the Cosmic Skull's audience and cemented their status as a distinctive voice in contemporary rock.
